newsitem.title: TAIWAN: For Taiwan, S.Africa snub shows China's long reach.
newsitem.headline: For Taiwan, S.Africa snub shows China's long reach.

text.p: For Taiwan, South Africa's plan to sever ties with the island is a painful reminder of something made abundantly clear by China's intimidating war games earlier this year -- Beijing ultimately calls the shots.
Wherever Taiwan turns, whether in foreign trade, investment, diplomacy, arms procurement or even domestic policy, China and its containment policy are there setting the ground rules.
"Communist China is demonstrating to Taiwan that it has too many bargaining chips besides military power," said National Taiwan University political scientist Timothy Ting.

Many Taiwan officials have long conceded in private it was only a matter of time before South African President Nelson Mandela would accede to Chinese pressure and order the step he announced on Wednesday -- a shift of ties from Taipei.
But most had clung to Mandela's comments that it would be "immoral" to abandon a friend.
Analysts said Mandela was getting nowhere with his effort to maintain ties with "both Chinas", a political heresy to Beijing, and could no longer resist China's enormous economic allure.
Veteran Taiwan-watcher Jean-Pierre Cabestan said Beijing appeared to have singled out Pretoria for special pressure.

"Mainland China has renewed its offensive in Africa," he said. "The pressure (on Pretoria) has been very strong in the last couple of months, in particular because of the return of Hong Kong to China" in mid-1997.
Another National Taiwan University expert, Hu Fo, said Beijing's success with Pretoria could have wide repercussions.
"There could be some chain reaction in Africa because Mandela is so much respected in Africa and whatever his government does will have a big infuence there," Hu said.
South Africa is the biggest of just 30 countries -- mostly underdeveloped states in central America and Africa -- that recognise Taiwan rather than the communist People's Republic.

Since the vanquished Chinese Nationalist government fled into exile on Taiwan in 1949, Beijing's communist leaders have pushed incessantly to recover Taiwan, shelling its outer islands in the early years and squeezing it diplomatically.

Taiwan has worked equally diligently to resist communist domination, mounting one of Asia's most respected armies with U.S. help and later using the muscle of its "Asian dragon" economy to ride out its growing isolation.

After Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui visited the United States privately in mid-1995 despite a lack of formal U.S. ties, Beijing turned up the heat sharply, mounting war games and missile tests that reached a climax on the eve of Taiwan's historic March presidential election.
Beijing's message then, as now, was clear: Taiwan has no right to sovereign ties or political independence and one day will be reunified with the mainland.
South Africa's move further squeezes Taiwan, which has not been able to talk even informally with Beijing since Lee's U.S. trip sent cautious semi-official links into a tailspin.
"This is a huge setback for Taiwan and will have a big effect on the people's morale," said university expert Hu Fo.
"Taiwan is at its wits' end. It is losing friends and the core problem is Beijing but Beijing does not want to talk."

Ting said the South Africa blow -- and the groundbreaking U.S.-China summit of presidents Bill Clinton and Jiang Zemin -- could force Taiwan to rethink its policy of seeking "international space" and a seat in the United Nations, moves seen by China as provocative.

"This is another major blow for Taiwan and the pragmatic diplomacy promoted by President Lee Teng-hui...," Ting said. "It shows...pragmatic diplomacy is moving towards a dead end. The policy has cost us our last major diplomatic ally."
Taipei itself is clear about its adversary, but insisted Beijing's pressure would be counterproductive.
"The origin of this issue is communist China," government spokesman Su Chi quoted Premier Lien Chan as saying.

"This shows communist China is intensifying its repression of us internationally. Its moves to buy foreign relations will not do any good to cross-strait relations or national reunification," Lien was quoted as saying.
